Antique Embroidery and Vernacular Furniture & Works of Art from the Collection of Ian and Barbara Kennedy-MartinA Charles II silk embroidered, metal thread and beaded Biblical picture, probably depicting Moses' marriage to Zipporah

Third quarter 17th century 
Embroidered with the continuous story of Moses' marriage to Zipporah, including the meeting at a well to the lower left, and Moses receiving his bride to the right, all enclosed by an elaborate zoological and foliate border, in a later moulded frame, size including the frame: 55cm wide, 6cm deep, 40.5cm high (21 1/2in wide, 2in deep, 15 1/2in high) (the embroidery: 38.5cm wide x 24cm high)

Provenance:

Conserved by Jennifer Gill in 1984 according to a receipt

Moses first encountered Zipporah in Midian as he was fleeing Egypt for killing an Egyptian taskmaster. He protected her and her six sisters from aggressive shepherds while he was resting by a well. Grateful for his help, the women's father Jethro invited Moses for a meal and offered him Zipporah's hand in marriage.

description_block:
Antique Embroidery and Vernacular Furniture & Works of Art from the Collection of Ian and Barbara Kennedy-MartinA Charles II mythological silk raised-work embroidered picture
Dated 1679 
Depicting Actaeon with his antlers to the right of the central oval cartouche, the whole with silk and metal threads, initiated 'D.C', in a later carved frame, size including the frame: 55.5cm wide, 4cm deep, 39.5cm high (21 1/2in wide, 1 1/2in deep, 15 1/2in high) (the embroidery: 49cm wide x 32.5cm high)

In Greek mythology, Actaeon was a celebrated hunter who incurred the wrath of the goddess Artemis (Diana) after inadvertently coming upon her while she bathed. As punishment, Artemis transformed him into a stag, the metamorphosis beginning with a pair of antlers emerging from his head. As recounted in Ovid's Metamorphoses, Actaeon gradually assumed the form of a deer and, unable to speak or reveal his identity, fled in terror. He was ultimately pursued and torn apart by his own hunting hounds, who failed to recognise their master in his altered guise.

Conserved by Jennifer Gill, Bristol according to a label verso

description_block:
Antique Embroidery and Vernacular Furniture & Works of Art from the Collection of Ian and Barbara Kennedy-MartinA Charles II embroidered picture of Abraham, Sarah, and the three angels
Dated May 30 1681
In coloured wools depicting Abraham on his knees whilst Sarah is depicted to the right of the work hiding in her tent, and initialled 'RS, ES, AS', as well as indistinct words and numbers to the borders, within a later ebonised frame, size including the frame: 71cm wide, 3cm deep, 49.5cm high (27 1/2in wide, 1in deep, 19in high) (the embroidery: 59cm wide x 37.5cm high)

Provenance:
With Avon Antiques, Bradford-on-Avon, where acquired in 1984

Conserved by Jennifer Gill, Bristol according to a receipt. 

The above embroidery depicts the Old Testament story of Abraham and Sarah receiving the three angels (Genesis 18). Abraham is shown kneeling before three mysterious visitors, offering them hospitality and refreshment, while Sarah appears in the background, listening from the entrance of her tent. Upon hearing the angels foretell that she will bear a son in her old age, Sarah laughs in disbelief, a pivotal moment in the biblical narrative.
artwork_title: A Charles II embroidered picture of Abraham, Sarah, and the three angels
provenance: With Avon Antiques, Bradford-on-Avon, where acquired in 1984. Conserved by Jennifer Gill, Bristol according to a receipt.
subject_matter: Abraham, Sarah, three angels, tent, tree, hospitality, garment colors, biblical narrative, figures, landscape

Gower Peninsula, mid-18th century

Provenance:

This rare coffor bach (Welsh for 'little coffer') forms part of a small and distinctive group of coffers associated with the Gower Peninsula in South Wales. Havard, The Gower Coffor Bach, Regional Furniture, vol. VI (1992). For a comparable example, see Woolley & Wallis, The Age of Oak, 14 January 2025, lot 47.

Made by John Peck and Son
Stamped with the initials 'A.R.J' to the lid enclosing a black Moroccan leather lined interior, with a calling card for 'Mr. Charles Wingfield: His Britannic Majesty's Envoy Extraordinary and Minister Plenipotentiary', and written in pen 'Major A. Reid Jamieson', 40cm wide, 27cm deep, 14cm high (15 1/2in wide, 10 1/2in deep, 5 1/2in high)

Major Alan Reid Jamieson served as Secretary to the Irish Grants Committee in the 1920s, the British government body established to assess and administer compensation claims submitted by Southern Irish loyalists who suffered loss of property, displacement, intimidation, or violence during and after the Irish War of Independence (1919-21) and the Irish Civil War (1922-23). In this role, Jamieson played a central part in reviewing claims and recommending awards, making him a significant figure in the distribution of financial relief to Irish refugees and loyalists in the early years of the Irish Free State.

description_block:
The Collection of the Late P.D. CarterNaÃ¯ve School, 19th century
The Wild Ox of Chillingham with Castle and the Eildons in the distance 
oil on canvas
37 x 53cm (14 9/16 x 20 7/8in).

This is a rare depiction of an animal from the Chillingham herd, most famously painted by Sir Edward Landseer (Wild cattle of Chillingham, painted in 1867).

The Chillingham cattle are a rare breed of wild white cattle that have inhabited Chillingham Park in Northumberland for centuries. They have been enclosed in Chillingham Park since the 13th or 14th century, and considered to be the sole survivors of the ancient British forest herds. They are recognisable by their white coats, dark muzzles and characteristically long horns. Living as a largely unmanaged, closed herd, they retain a unique genetic heritage and offer a remarkable insight into the history of Britain's native cattle. Today, they remain an important part of the country's natural and cultural heritage. There is a population of around 120-138 animals in the herd and they are completely wild, having never been touched by human hands or received any veterinary care, it is remarkable that they exist wildly on the Scottish borders.

description_block:
The Collection of the Late P.D. CarterA painted panel of the arms of the Scottish family of Robertson of Pitmillan (Aberdeenshire)
Together with a 19th century framed needlework family armorial for the Scottish family of Houstoun of Calderhall, co. Edinburgh, 42 x 37.5cm (16 9/16 x 14 3/4in) The needlework panel: 21 x 16cm, (2)

The painted panel: 

These are the arms of the Scottish family of ROBERTSON of Pitmillan (Aberdeenshire). They are ancient descendants of the Duke of Atholl. The original family of ROBERTSON, Chiefs of Clan Donnachaidh, have arms that included three wolves' heads on a red background. The version we see here is much differenced and in 1763 was exemplified by the Court of Lord Lyon for the use of this particular branch of the family.

Notably a John ROBERTSON of Pitmillan, merchant was provost of Aberdeen 1736-8 and still present there in 1760. 

The blazon:

argent, on a chief gules three wolves heads erased of the first and in base a chaplet vert all within a bordure counter-company also of the first and azure.

Motto: VIRTUTIS GLORIA MERCES (also used by the parent clan).

The embroidered armorial:

These are the arms of the Scottish family of HOUSTOUN of Calderhall, co. Edinburgh that were matriculated in 1799 at the Court of Lord Lyon in Scotland. The family were later HOUSTON, who in 1836 were created Baronets and later 1847 assumed the arms and family name by royal licence of HOUSTON-BOSWALL. This dates the embroidery in the period 1799-1847.

Notably General Sir William HOUSTON (1766-1842) KGCB was created in 1836 Baronet and Governor of Gibraltar. 

The blazon:

or, a chevron chequy argent and sable between three martlets of the last.

Motto: IN TIME

With thanks to Roger Whitworth in the identification of these arms.

description_block:
The Personal Archive of Peter AfiaA panel of French silk chinÃ©, together with seven French printed toiles, and another
Early 19th century and later
The chinÃ© with three partridges between wreathed garlands of flowers entwined with ears of wheat, one selvedge, three edges machine stitched, together with:
a variety of 19th and 20th century French printed toiles, to include 
a valence of Empire-style printed toile de Jouy depicting Pallas and Venus, probably from the Oberkampf manufactory, circa 1810;
a Neoclassical panel of toile de Jouy depicting L'Histoire de PsychÃ©, with Dimitrios label, after the original design by Jean-Baptiste Huet for the Oberkampf manufactory, circa 1810;
a quilted panel of Le Bal, a figurative toile d'Alsace, roller-printed in rose pink, Mulhouse, France, circa 1845;
a part quilt of printed cotton toile, printed in deep red with medallions of winged mythological figures, backed with linen, French, early 19th century, etc.
the part quilt: 250cm x 69cm (9)

The first, with three partridges, appears to be based on the design of brocaded silk, The Partridges (Les Perdrix), by the workshop of Philippe de Lasalle, woven in Lyon circa 1770 and used by Catherine the Great (see V and A T.187-1931). This chiné version may be later.

The Pallas and Venus example is the source inspiration for the 'Aphrodite' Marvic Textiles design.

description_block:
The Personal Archive of Peter AfiaA table cover of embroidered linen
American, early 20th century, possibly Deerfield Massachusetts
Worked in blue linen with four urns of flowers in a quartered field, with a lace border, together with:
a joined panel of hand-woven striped indigo linen, possibly French, circa 1900, affixed with label inscribed 'New Checked/Stripe - Original/Document';
a panel of figured velvet, woven with a hexagonal lattice of flower sprigs, with old 'Magasin' label inscribed 'Velours Chais bleu';
and a shaped panel of printed cotton twill, mounted on card, with Marvic Textiles label inscribed 'Geometric Tree Design/American Design/Circa 1930's-1940's'
the table cover approx.: 125cm x 175cm (4)

The table cover is thought to be from Deerfield, Massachusetts where blue and white embroidery was characteristic of the Arts and Crafts revival at the turn of the century. This appears to have been the source inspiration for the 'Tuileries 1420' Marvic Textiles design.

The hand-woven striped indigo linen appears to be a source document for the later 'Bercy 1424' Marvic Textiles design.
